subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Gene expression is the process by which:
choices: A gene is copied before cell division
Genes are passed from parents to their offspring in gametes
New alleles are formed by mutation
The information in a gene is used to make a product such as a protein
items.note: Expression = transcription (and translation) of the gene's information into a functional product.

choices: Bind to DNA and increase or decrease transcription of genes
Join amino acids together at the ribosome
Remove introns from pre-mRNA in the nucleus before export
Copy DNA during the S phase of the cell cycle
items.note: They bind near promoters or at enhancers and control whether RNA polymerase can transcribe.

items.stem: Monozygotic (identical) twins can develop different traits over their lives mainly because of:
choices: Differences in the base sequences of their genomes
Independent assortment of chromosomes during their early development
Differences in gene expression caused by their environment
Crossing over in their body cells
items.note: Their DNA sequences are essentially the same; epigenetic and environmental differences alter which genes are expressed.

items.stem: Methylation of cytosine bases in a gene's promoter usually:
choices: Increases transcription of the gene
Reduces transcription of the gene
Changes the amino acid sequence coded
Converts cytosine into thymine permanently
items.note: Methyl groups on DNA (CpG sites) block transcription factors and attract proteins that condense chromatin.

choices: More condensed, so genes are silenced
Less condensed, so genes are more easily transcribed
Break into separate nucleosomes that leave the nucleus
Bind more tightly to the DNA, removing the promoter
items.note: Acetyl groups neutralise positive charges on histones, loosening their grip on DNA and opening it for transcription.

choices: The full base sequence of all the genes in a cell
The complete set of all proteins made by a cell at any one time
All the mRNA molecules made by a cell at one time
The pattern of chemical tags on DNA and histones that affects expression
items.note: Epigenetic marks change expression without changing the base sequence. The proteome is the set of proteins; the transcriptome the RNA.

items.stem: Lactose in the surroundings of E. coli causes the genes for lactose metabolism to be expressed. This shows that:
choices: The environment can change gene expression
Genes mutate in response to what an organism needs
Bacteria can choose which genes they inherit
Lactose is converted into new DNA by the bacterium
items.note: Lactose binds to a repressor, releasing it from DNA, so the genes are transcribed only when needed.

items.stem: A steroid hormone such as oestradiol changes gene expression in its target cells by:
choices: Binding to the cell surface and adding methyl groups to every gene in the nucleus
Being translated at ribosomes into proteins that replace the cell's own DNA
Entering the cell and binding a receptor that then acts as a transcription factor
Changing the base sequence of the genes that the cell transcribes
items.note: Steroids pass through the membrane; the hormone–receptor complex binds DNA and alters transcription of specific genes.

items.stem: Most epigenetic tags are removed in gametes and early embryos, but some are inherited. The best evidence for inheritance of epigenetic marks is that:
choices: The offspring have new mutations in their genes
Offspring always have the same phenotype as their parents
DNA sequences change in each generation
Effects of a parent's environment are seen in offspring without DNA sequence changes
items.note: Studies (e.g. famine exposure) show effects passed on that are not explained by base-sequence change.

items.stem: Different cell types in one organism have different transcriptomes but the same genome. This is because:
choices: Each cell type has permanently lost the genes it does not use
Each cell type expresses a different subset of its genes
Each cell type contains different chromosomes
Each cell type mutates its genome as it develops
items.note: Differentiation depends on gene regulation (transcription factors, epigenetic marks), not loss of DNA.

items.stem: Air pollution has been linked to changes in DNA methylation in some people. A likely consequence is:
choices: Altered expression of genes, which might affect health
A change in the base sequence of every gene affected
Inheritance of new alleles by all of the person's children
Immediate death of the cells exposed to the pollutant
items.note: Environmental factors can change methylation patterns, altering expression (e.g. of genes linked to inflammation) without mutating DNA.

items.stem: Explain how DNA methylation can control gene expression.
markscheme: Methyl groups are added to cytosine (CpG sites) in or near promoters (1)
Chromatin becomes more condensed, so the gene is not transcribed (silenced) (1)
items.tactic: Mechanism questions: chemical change → effect on binding → effect on transcription.

items.stem: Distinguish between the genome, the transcriptome and the proteome.
markscheme: Genome = all the genetic information/DNA of an organism (the same in all body cells) (1)
Transcriptome = all the RNA transcribed in a cell at a given time (1)
Proteome = all the proteins produced by a cell/organism at a given time; both vary with cell type and time (1)
items.tactic: Define each term in one line, then state what varies.

items.stem: Outline how environmental factors can affect gene expression, using one named example.
markscheme: Environment affects which genes are transcribed (or epigenetic tags) (1)
Named example, e.g. temperature and fur colour in Himalayan rabbits / lactose and the lac genes (1)
Explanation of mechanism for the example (e.g. heat-sensitive enzyme for pigment inactive at body core temperature) (1)
items.tactic: Name the example early, then link cause → mechanism → phenotype.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) DNA methylation (%) of a gene promoter and the gene's mRNA level (arbitrary units) were measured in 5 tissues: A 10%, 95; B 25%, 70; C 50%, 40; D 70%, 18; E 90%, 4.
(a) Describe the relationship. (b) Suggest an explanation. (c) State why a correlation alone does not prove that methylation causes the change.
markscheme: (a) Negative correlation: as methylation increases from 10% to 90%, mRNA falls from 95 to 4 (1)
(b) Methylation blocks the binding of transcription factors/RNA polymerase, so less transcription (1)
(c) Another factor could cause both (e.g. histone modification) / correlation does not show cause; experiments that change methylation are needed (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
